title: Stall suppression probe: proxy drain + pacing experiments
content:
Context and motivation:

This is a set of lab notes for a focused microbenchmark series exploring how downstream proxy drain behavior and pacing knobs affect streaming tail latency and stall symptoms in our inference path. We care because customers are seeing rare "stalls" (multi-second tails) on streaming responses that correlate with proxy chains and bursts from client-side flush patterns. The goal here is not to be exhaustive but to expose plausible mechanisms and inexpensive mitigations we can ship in the proxy/ingress stack.

Summary of hypothesis:
- When a proxy(s) performs aggressive connection-level drain or coalesces writes, it can create pauses that interact poorly with downstream server's bursty token production and KV-cache warmup, producing observable stalls at token boundaries.
- A pacing/drain-smoothing layer on the proxy can reduce tail latency at the cost of small median increases.
- Behavior differs by transport (HTTP/1.1 chunked, HTTP/2 multiplexed frames, gRPC streaming over HTTP/2) and by client flush pattern (micro-flush vs batched).

High-level experimental setup:
- Workload: synthetic streaming generator (client) that simulates autocompletion output produced by runtime. Configurable token rate and burstiness.
- Server: local dev server running inference runtime in dev mode (no GPU) to keep per-token production deterministic. Added artificial token compute time to emulate real work (random 3-8ms/token).
- Proxy: our in-house edge proxy (dev build) with knobs: drain-window-ms, burst-coalesce-threshold-bytes, pacing-rate (tokens/s equivalent), and write-buffering-enabled flag.
- Client runner: custom Go harness (wrk-like) that supports HTTP/1.1 chunked streaming, HTTP/2 server-push style framing, and gRPC streaming. Emits flush patterns: single-token-flush (every token flushed), batch-8, batch-32.
- Measurement: collect per-stream token arrival timestamps at the client, end-to-end response time, 95/99/99.9p latencies, and tcpdump traces. Also capture proxy and server logs with request ids.

Experiment matrix (kept small):
- Transports: http1-chunked, http2-framed, grpc-stream
- Proxy modes: baseline (no pacing), drain-smoothing(50ms window), pacing(200 tokens/s), coalesce-threshold(8KB)
- Client flush: token, batch-8, batch-32

Key observations (raw):
1) HTTP/1.1 chunked + token-flush: baseline shows pronounced microstall spikes at 99.9p. TCP traces show short pause in data from proxy (40-120ms) immediately after bursts of small writes. These line up with proxy write aggregation and downstream socket backpressure.
2) HTTP/2 + token-flush: better than http1 at medians, but 99.9p still spikes. Multiplexing reduces head-of-line effects, but frame coalescing in proxy induced backpressure bursts across streams.
3) gRPC streaming: shows the most consistent tails in baseline; gRPC's internal windowing interacts with proxy-level coalescing to create pacing mismatches.

Effects of knobs:
- drain-smoothing(50ms): reduces 99.9p tails by ~60% for http1 token-flush cases, at median cost ~+2ms. The smoothing prevents large instantaneous write bursts from leaving proxy buffers, so downstream sees steadier packet flow.
- pacing(200 tokens/s): for workloads with server-side token jitter, pacing reduces stalls but increased median latency by ~6-10ms. Best for applications that prefer stable tails over absolute medians.
- coalesce-threshold(8KB): for batch-32 workloads, raising threshold improved throughput but for token-flush it made tails worse (more coalescing => larger pauses). So threshold must be workload-aware.

Representative numbers (compiled from runs, per-1000-stream batch):
- HTTP/1.1, token-flush, baseline: median=18ms, 95p=42ms, 99.9p=420ms
- HTTP/1.1, token-flush, drain-smooth: median=20ms, 95p=38ms, 99.9p=170ms
- HTTP/2, token-flush, baseline: median=14ms, 95p=36ms, 99.9p=200ms
- gRPC, token-flush, baseline: median=22ms, 95p=50ms, 99.9p=560ms

Trace-level notes:
- tcpdump on server network interface shows a repeating pattern: a cluster of small packets then a quiet gap ~60-120ms then next cluster. When drain-smoothing was enabled, packet spacing became more regular and clusters smaller.
- Proxy logs show "write_coalesce triggered" events aligned with the pauses. The proxy's write loop used a non-adaptive flush policy that triggered flush when buffer > 4KB OR every 10ms. This interacts badly with token-flush patterns where many small writes arrive in <10ms.

Instrumenting the server's socket write path:
- Added per-request counters for write syscall latency and bytes per write. Observed server write syscalls are usually small (<256B) when token-flush, which exacerbates syscall cost as well. Notably, when proxy coalesced, server write syscalls returned EAGAIN occasionally and we observed the server entering a short epoll wakeup cycle.

Root causes (synthesis):
1) Mismatch between client flush granularity and proxy flush policy causes bursts that then interact with kernel-level transmit scheduling and downstream TCP window to create inter-cluster pauses.
2) Multiplexing (http2) reduces some head-of-line but does not eliminate the underlying issue when proxy coalesces across streams.
3) gRPC's flow control and larger in-flight windows means when a pause occurs it affects more tokens in flight, producing larger tails.

Practical mitigations tested and recommended (cheap → expensive):
- Default: enable small drain-smoothing window on edge proxy (e.g., 20-50ms). Low risk, reduces 99.9p in many token-flush workloads.
- Adaptive coalesce threshold: proxy detects average payload size / flush frequency per-client and switches coalesce thresholds. This reduced worst-case tails in mixed workloads.
- Server-side write batching: aggregate 2-4 tokens before issuing syscall when CPU allows; trades tiny median increase for fewer small syscalls and smaller proxy-visible bursts. Needs experiment for memory/latency tradeoffs.
- gRPC-specific: tune initial window sizes and max frame sizes for streaming endpoints. Smaller windows reduced the blast radius of a single proxy pause.
- Longer-term: consider a pacing token at the ingress that applies a small jitter to outgoing frames to avoid synchronous bursts across many client connections (this would be an opt-in feature).

Open questions and follow-ups:
- Does this reproduce on real GPU-backed model servers when token production variability is larger? (Next step: run representative model on a small cluster.)
- How do cloud load-balancers (L4) change behavior vs our proxy? Initial quick tests show L4 pass-through reduces coalescing but increases connection churn; needs more study.
- Should we expose a "burst profile" hint in API/SDK so clients can declare their flush patterns and proxies can tune per-connection policies?

Short TODOs (next runs):
- Run one representative full-model test (gpt-mini config) with and without drain-smoothing to validate behavior under heavier token jitter (owner: Sara, due 2024-04-22).
- Add server-side per-socket backpressure counters to correlate EAGAIN events with observed stalls (owner: Liam, due 2024-04-19).
- Prototype adaptive coalesce threshold heuristic in proxy (owner: Ethan, spike by 2024-04-29).

Notes to reviewers:
- This doc contains rough numbers from lab and should be treated as experimental. I removed detailed raw logs to keep file small; see linked PR for test harness and raw captures.
- If we decide to ship drain-smoothing as default, we should add it behind a rollout flag for Dedicated/Private tenants to evaluate perf tradeoffs.

Appendix: quick commands used (dev harness)
- start client runner (http1 token flush): go run ./bench/client -mode http1 -flush token -streams 1000 -duration 60s -server http://proxy:8080/stream
- tcpdump capture: sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -w /tmp/trace.pcap port 8080 and host 10.0.2.5
- extract token timestamps: scripts/parse_timestamps.py /tmp/trace.pcap > /tmp/timestamps.csv

Raw config knobs (proxy-dev):
- write_coalesce_bytes = 4096 (default)
- write_coalesce_ms = 10 (default)
- drain_smooth_ms = 0 (default, turned to 50 for tests)
- pacing_rate_tokens_per_sec = 0 => disabled (set to 200 for pacing test)

End.
